framework: Professor Adow TVET — Digital Skills for the Workshop
note: A CORE module, not a trade one. Every department in this school now meets a computer at work — a moisture meter in agriculture, an inverter in welding, a diagnostic tool in automotive, a controller on a chiller — and none of them is called a computer. The module teaches what is common to all of them rather than any one manufacturer's menus, because the menus change and input-process-store-output does not.
source: Topic scope follows the Ehel Academy Computing modules for Stages 1 and 2 (computers everywhere; networks and the internet; connected devices; hardware, software and robots). NOTHING is ported: those are written for six- and seven-year-olds, and every criterion here is rewritten for an adult at grade 8-11 working in a trade.

assessmentModes.knowledge: Assessable by the platform: identification, reasoning, written answer.
assessmentModes.both: Taught and practised here; signed off on real equipment by an assessor.
assessmentModes.practical: Bench or site only. The platform can teach it and cannot assess it.

weightingNote: Digital skills sit at the opposite end from carpentry: most of this module IS assessable on screen, because naming a part, choosing wired over wireless and ordering a diagnosis are judgements rather than hand skills. The one criterion that can only be signed off at a machine is the safety one, and that is the right one to be strict about.

modules.title: Digital Skills for the Workshop
modules.description: What a computer is and where it hides in trade equipment; how a site gets connected and what to do when it does not; hardware, software and the machines that act on their own.

criteria.text: Name the four things every computer does — take input, process it, store it, give output — and point to each one on a device used in your own trade.
Identify the computer inside a piece of equipment that is not called a computer: a moisture meter, a welding inverter, a vehicle diagnostic tool, a milk chiller, a feed scale.
criteria.evidence: Identification task from photographs or real equipment.

criteria.text: Distinguish a general-purpose computer from an embedded one, and explain why a machine's controller cannot simply be used for something else.
Separate a mechanical fault from a digital one on the same machine, and say which trade attends to each.
State what data a workplace device holds, who it belongs to, and what may not be copied or removed from it.
Start up, log in to and shut down a shared workshop computer without losing another person's work.
Report a device fault so a technician can act on it: what was being done, what happened, what was expected instead.
criteria.evidence: Written fault report assessed against a rubric.

criteria.text: Distinguish a local network from the internet, and name one job on site that needs each.
Identify the parts of a small site network — the device, the access point or router, and the line leaving the building — and say what each one does.
Choose wired or wireless for a stated job and justify the choice by reliability, distance and interference.
Connect a device to a named network, and recognise when you have joined the wrong one.
criteria.evidence: Observed on a device; screenshot evidence.

criteria.text: Diagnose a connection failure in order: the device is off the network, the network has no route out, or the service itself is down.
State what must never be sent over a shared or public connection, and why a password typed on site is not private by default.
Describe how a job's records reach the office, and what happens to them if the connection drops mid-shift.

units.title: Hardware, software and machines that act

criteria.text: Separate hardware from software on a device you use, and say which of the two a given fault is likely to sit in.
Describe what settings and firmware are, and why a machine can behave differently after an update.
Name the three parts of an automated machine — sensor, controller, actuator — and trace a signal through them from a real example.
Distinguish a machine that repeats a fixed sequence from one that responds to what a sensor reads.
Work safely around an automated machine, including treating a stopped machine as one that may still start.
criteria.evidence: Supervised observation; signed off at the machine.

criteria.text: Judge which tasks in your trade a machine does better than a person, and which it does not, giving a reason from the work itself.
Record a machine's settings before changing them, and restore them afterwards.
